Living Well / Essay

Choosing between two good lives

Essay · 3 min read · Published October 8, 2026

On this page
  1. Name what is good about each possibility
  2. An attractive plan is not yet a livable plan
  3. Let tools expose assumptions rather than assign values
  4. A reversible step may be enough for now
  5. A good decision can still lead to disappointment
  6. Respect what the choice leaves behind
  7. One question to take with you

Some decisions are difficult because both possibilities contain something you genuinely value. A clearer process can help without turning the tradeoff into a hidden multiple-choice test.

Name what is good about each possibility

Consider a hypothetical choice between an absorbing opportunity and greater availability for existing commitments. It is possible to value both. Describing one as ambition and the other as fear, or one as responsibility and the other as selfishness, may settle the language before you have examined the actual decision.

Give each option a fair account. What would become possible? What would be harder? Who would be affected? A useful comparison should not require making the unchosen life sound foolish or unworthy.

An attractive plan is not yet a livable plan

Imagine the option on an ordinary day, not only on the day you feel most capable. Consider the actual time, resources, responsibilities, and maintenance it requires. Check any assumptions about other people's cooperation with those people.

Ask what happens when the week is less convenient than expected. A plan may need more slack, a smaller scope, or a clear exit. Practical fit is not a failure of aspiration; it is part of making an aspiration honest enough to act on.

Let tools expose assumptions rather than assign values

A comparison table can reveal missing information. An AI conversation can offer alternative questions or point out a possible inconsistency. Neither should decide how much a relationship, responsibility, or personal commitment is worth to you.

Use the values-before-advice guide before asking for a recommendation. Keep uncertainty visible. A precise-looking ranking can still rest on invented numbers or preferences that were never yours.

A reversible step may be enough for now

Where the stakes and circumstances permit, you may be able to test a smaller version of an option before making a larger commitment. Define what you want to learn and what the trial would not reveal. Include the effect on other people and agree on their involvement.

Not every choice can be tested this way. Some commitments have real deadlines or irreversible consequences. In those cases, clearer information and appropriate advice matter more than forcing the situation into the language of experimentation.

A good decision can still lead to disappointment

An outcome contains information, but it is not the entire measure of the original decision. Review what was known, which assumptions were reasonable, which checks were missed, and what changed later. A disappointing result may reveal a process problem, bad luck, or both.

Poker offers one useful reminder that a decision and its result are not identical. Personal life, however, is not a poker model: probabilities may be unknown, values are not reducible to chips, and the people affected are not pieces in a game. The existing decision-quality note explores the distinction through explicitly worked examples.

Respect what the choice leaves behind

Choosing one worthwhile possibility can involve a genuine loss of another. That loss does not necessarily mean the choice was wrong. You can acknowledge it without endlessly reopening the decision or pretending that every path would have led to the same life.

Keep a brief record of your reasons and a sensible review point where appropriate. Revising a plan in response to real information is different from treating every difficult day as evidence that you chose the wrong identity.

One optional practice

Write one fair paragraph about each option, including what you value and what you would give up. Then describe one ordinary day under each plan. Check which details are facts and which are assumptions.

Keep any notes privately. Skip or adapt this exercise if it does not fit your circumstances.

One question to take with you

Which tradeoff can you acknowledge honestly, rather than accepting only if you can persuade yourself it is not a tradeoff?
